newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egyptian real estate shares overvalued - CMA boss.
newsitem.headline: Egyptian real estate shares overvalued - CMA boss.

text.p: The chairman of Egypt's Capital Market Authority (CMA) said in an interview published on Saturday that investors had overvalued some real estate shares and that some recent stock price rises were unhealthy.
The Egyptian all-share index has risen 40 percent since the start of this year and 103 percent in the past 12 months.
Two partially privatised real estate companies, Medinet Nasr and Heliopolis Housing and Development, have been among the star performers.

Abdelhamid Ibrahim told the government newspaper al-Ahram that investors had driven up the price of real estate shares in the belief that the companies could make quick profits from their holdings of valuable land.

"People have been rushing to buy shares in such companies because they expect the value of the land they own will increase greatly and the companies will make big profits from the difference between the book value and the market value.

"What they don't realise is that this land is just a commodity which cannot be sold in a year, for example. This might take years. This has made the shares in the real estate companies rise more than necessary," he said.

Medinet Nasr shares, sold to the public last May at 65 pounds, peaked at 500 pounds in January but have since fallen back to 450 pounds. Heliopolis Housing shares reached 650 in January and last traded at 490.

Talking of the share market in general, Ibrahim said: "I am not happy with the price jumps although there are justifications for them. The price jumps are not a natural phenomenon... They are not a healthy phenomenon whatever the reasons, because a gradual advance is what's natural."
But he said that the Cairo market was still relatively cheap, given the low P/E ratios, low inflation, falling interest rates and improvements in the speed of transactions.
"I say that the occurrence of a crisis is not a possibility on the Egyptian exchange," he added. The situation was different from Kuwait in the early 1980s and Mexico in 1994, he said.
Ibrahim suggested investors take another look at the bond market, which has lost much of its appeal because of the rapid price rises in the equities market.
"It's my duty to advise the public at this point that bonds are an important element in any portfolio...because they are relatively stable compared with shares," he said.

He dismissed press speculation that price manipulations were behind some recent share price increases but he said the exchange last week suspended one broker for three months for submitting a fictitous order for shares at a price 50 pounds above the opening price. He did not give details.
"I cannot say that this (price manipulation) does not happen but it does not have much effect," he added.
